content: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are prevalent in both men and women, as demonstrated by population-based studies. These symptoms impose significant personal and societal burdens. According to the International Continence Society (ICS), LUTS can be broadly categorized into storage symptoms, voiding symptoms, and post-micturition symptoms. Voiding symptoms, while more common in men, are also frequently observed in women. Voiding dysfunction is defined by the ICS and the International Urogynecological Association as abnormally slow and/or incomplete urination, diagnosed through symptoms and urodynamic investigations. Female voiding dysfunction specifically refers to difficulties in emptying the bladder, which may result from ineffective detrusor (bladder muscle) contractions, obstruction of bladder outflow, loss of coordination between the detrusor and sphincter muscles, or a combination of these factors. The prevalence of voiding symptoms in women has been reported as 19.5% in a large European study (EPIC), while other studies have shown prevalence rates of 7.2% to 12.8% among female urology patients visiting clinics. In a survey of 15,861 women over 40 years old in the US, UK, and Sweden, terminal dribbling was the most common symptom (38.3%), followed by a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying (27.4%) and a weak urinary stream (20.1%). Female voiding dysfunction is complex, poorly understood, and challenging to treat. There is no consensus on its standard definition, diagnosis, or management. It often remains untreated until patients present with severe symptoms such as urine retention, renal insufficiency, recurrent urinary tract infections, or overflow incontinence, particularly in cases of bladder outlet obstruction. LUTS negatively impact multiple domains of health-related quality of life, including general health perception, mental health, and overall bladder function. Women with voiding dysfunction experience higher levels of depression and anxiety compared to asymptomatic controls, with significantly higher bother scores in women than men. Voiding dysfunction symptoms often coexist with storage symptoms such as frequency, urgency, and nocturia, complicating diagnosis and management. These symptoms are also commonly associated with post-micturition symptoms, and women may report concurrent stress and urgency urinary incontinence. Voiding dysfunction is linked to aging, pelvic organ prolapse, and a history of hysterectomy or continence surgery. The causes of female voiding dysfunction can be broadly divided into detrusor underactivity and bladder outlet obstruction (BOO). Detrusor underactivity is characterized by reduced strength and/or duration of bladder muscle contractions, leading to prolonged or incomplete bladder emptying. BOO refers to physical obstruction during voiding, characterized by increased detrusor pressure and reduced urine flow rate. Physiological causes of BOO include urogenital prolapse and urethral stricture, while iatrogenic causes include urethral trauma or surgery for continence or prolapse. Neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis or spinal cord compression may also present with altered voiding symptoms. Patients with voiding dysfunction should undergo a thorough evaluation, including urine analysis, uroflowmetry, and post-void residual urine measurement. If the free flow rate is abnormally low, filling cystometry with pressure-flow studies can help differentiate between detrusor underactivity and BOO. Urethral pressure profilometry may aid in diagnosing urethral stenosis or obstruction, while videocystourethrography can provide detailed information on lower urinary tract function and anatomy. Non-drug treatments for LUTS in women include pelvic floor muscle training, biofeedback, bladder training, behavioral modification, bladder reflex triggering, bladder expression, pessaries for pelvic organ prolapse, electrical or magnetic stimulation, and catheterization. These interventions are particularly valuable for patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to pharmacological therapies. Pelvic floor muscle training involves repetitive voluntary contraction and relaxation of specific pelvic floor muscles, while biofeedback provides patients with real-time information about physiological processes to improve muscle control. Bladder training aims to increase the time interval between voids to regain continence, and behavioral modification focuses on altering maladaptive voiding patterns. Electrical stimulation applies electrical currents to stimulate pelvic viscera or their nerve supply, while magnetic stimulation offers a non-invasive alternative with demonstrated short-term efficacy. Catheterization, either intermittent or indwelling, is used for bladder emptying in cases of severe dysfunction. Surgical interventions for voiding dysfunction include urethral dilation, urethrolysis, urethrotomy, bladder neck incisions, urethroplasty, partial cystectomy, sigmoid colon-cystoplasty, and continent urinary diversion. Urethrolysis may be preferable to urethral dilation, although it is not effective in resolving all symptoms. Mechanical obstruction due to urogenital prolapse can be relieved through surgery or intravaginal devices such as pessaries. Despite the availability of various non-drug treatments, there is a lack of consensus on the optimal management of female voiding dysfunction. Systematic reviews are needed to summarize the best available evidence and assess the cost-effectiveness of alternative treatment strategies.
